messages.author: a2bfdf24157fa01a
messages.subject: Parameterizing hierarchical shrinkage priors
parts:
Hi,

Ben mentioned during the StanCon Q&A that there were a lot of tricks in the rstanarm package to efficiently parameterize hierarchical shinkage priors. Unfortunately, I found the source files pretty obtuse - it seems the prior is split through several different files.

I thought I would beg for someone (Ben, Jonah, etc.) to give a quick rundown of the current thinking of how to parameterize these in a more human-readable format. I am familiar with the parameterization used by Piironen and Vehtari, but it sounded like there was something more efficient than that currently used by rstanarm.

Thanks in advance,

Matt

messages.author: 743bbacc59f4b25f
messages.subject: Re: Parameterizing hierarchical shrinkage priors
parts:
On Tuesday, January 24, 2017 at 2:24:04 PM UTC-5, Matt Espe wrote:
I thought I would beg for someone (Ben, Jonah, etc.) to give a quick rundown of the current thinking of how to parameterize these in a more human-readable format. I am familiar with the parameterization used by Piironen and Vehtari, but it sounded like there was something more efficient than that currently used by rstanarm.

Nice meeting you at StanCon. Here is a quick rundown. A lot of different kinds of priors are univariate normal with a particular function for the mean and / or standard deviation. In Stan (and rstanarm), we often use what is sometimes called a "non-centered (re)parameterization", which is basically just exploiting the fact that the normal distribution is in the scale-location family where

x = mu + sigma * z

where z is distributed standard normal, and thus x is distributed (a priori) normal with mean mu and standard deviation sigma.

It is especially important when using hierarchical shrinkage priors to use this non-centered (re)parameterization in order to make z the primitive(s) that you declare in the parameters block and x is declared and defined in the transformed parameters block. The posterior kernel in terms of x tends to change very rapidly, which makes it hard for NUTS to avoid divergent transitions, while the posterior kernel in terms of z tends to change slowly and NUTS is more likely to succeed.

The hs_prior and hsplus_prior functions are defined in

https://github.com/stan-dev/rstanarm/blob/master/inst/chunks/common_functions.stan

which basically just multiply a bunch of positive things together (that constitute sigma) and then multiply by z (mu is 0). The things whose product are sigma consist of fixed hyperparameters and unknown parameters that are declared in the parameters block. Under these hierarchical shrinkage priors, various things are supposed to have a half Student t prior, which specializes to a half Cauchy prior if the degrees of freedom are 1, which is what the original horseshoe literature did. A Student t variate with low degrees of freedom can also make things difficult for NUTS, which can manifest itself in either divergent transitions or a low BFMI. So, rstanarm exploits the fact that a Student t prior can be written as a scale-mixture of normals, where the mixing variable has a scaled, inverse, chi-squared prior, which is equivalent to a certain inverse gamma distribution. This is somewhere in BDA or see

https://www.johndcook.com//t_normal_mixture.pdf

So, wherever there is a half Student t, we multiply a half normal by something that is inverse gamma with both parameters equal to nu / 2 and marginally the product is Student t with nu degrees of freedom.

Then, you just have to remember to put the corresponding priors on all the primitive things (which are not even stored in rstanarm) such that the transformed parameters have the marginal distributions you want under these priors. This all takes place in the chunk

https://github.com/stan-dev/rstanarm/blob/master/inst/chunks/priors_glm.stan

Finally, you condition on the data and hope for the best. You will still probably get a lot of divergences unless adapt_delta is about 0.99.

Ben
